articles.title: CT and MRI in periprocedural transcatheter mitral valve replacement: expert recommendations by the European Society of Cardiovascular Radiology (ESCR) and the North American Society for Cardiovascular Imaging (NASCI).
articles.abstract: Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is a minimally invasive treatment option for symptomatic patients with severe mitral valve disease who are at high surgical risk or ineligible for open-heart surgery. The procedure has been associated with improved quality of life and functional status in selected patients and is increasingly recognized as a valuable therapeutic option in the management of complex mitral valve disorders. A multidisciplinary Heart Team is essential to ensure the clinical success of TMVR, and imaging specialists play a central role in the preprocedural assessment for patient and device selection, during the procedure, to guide and monitor the implantation, and after the procedure, for follow-up and for the correct diagnosis of short- or long-term complications. Echocardiography is required for initial diagnosis, for assessment of valve hemodynamics, intraprocedural guidance and monitoring. However, a multimodality approach including CT and/or MRI is frequently needed to correctly manage the phase of preprocedural planning and the diagnosis of complications. This consensus document, developed by a working group of experts from the European Society of Cardiovascular Radiology (ESCR) and the North American Society for Cardiovascular Imaging (NASCI), provides evidence-based recommendations for CT and cardiac MRI acquisition and post-processing in procedural planning and postprocedural evaluation in patients undergoing TMVR. Emphasis is placed on the technical requirements and standardization of imaging protocols, which must account for the heterogeneity of imaging equipment used in clinical settings. The document also outlines recommendations for all necessary preprocedural measures to ensure consistency, accuracy, and effective communication among specialists. KEY POINTS: Question How can CT and MRI acquisition, measurement, and reporting for TMVR be standardized to support accurate procedural planning, device selection, and follow-up? Findings This expert consensus provides recommendations for standardized CT and MRI protocols, key measurements, and structured reporting throughout TMVR planning and follow-up. Clinical relevance CT and MRI assessment may improve patient selection, procedural planning, multidisciplinary communication, and detection of postprocedural complications, supporting safer and more consistent TMVR practice across centers.

articles.title: Subcutaneous and Visceral Adipose Tissue Reference Values from the Framingham Heart Study Thoracic and Abdominal CT: Erratum.
Ulnar styloid osteolysis following distal radius fracture without ulnar fracture: frequency and associated factors.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the frequency and characteristics of ulnar styloid osteolysis after distal radius fracture without concomitant ulnar fracture. Secondary objectives were to assess associated risk factors and surgical outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective observational, single-center, radiographic cohort of adult patients diagnosed with distal radius fracture between July 1, 2018, and June 30, 2020, was reviewed. Ulnar styloid osteolysis was documented using wrist radiographs at diagnosis and follow-up. Patients with ulnar fractures or erosive arthropathy were excluded. Time to detection, size, morphology, location, and evolution of ulnar styloid osteolysis were recorded. Associations with patient and fracture characteristics were evaluated using Cox models. RESULTS: 143 patients (104 female, mean age 55.8 ± 17.6 years) were included. Ulnar styloid osteolysis was identified in 16.8% of patients (n = 24), with a median detection time of 56 days (range 24-386). Osteolysis was more likely in fractures with: comminution (83.3% vs. 59.7%, HR = 3.457 [1.145-9.845], p = 0.027), diastasis (33.3% vs. 10.1%, HR = 3.905 [1.646-9.266], p = 0.002), dorsal angulation (79.2% vs. 24.4%, HR 4.766 [1.619-14.035], p < 0.001), impaction (66.7% vs. 17.6%, HR = 5.823 [2.486-15.647], p < 0.001) and active smoking (35.5% vs. 16.5%, HR = 2.650 [1.054-6.665], p = 0.038). Osteolysis was more frequently observed in patients who underwent surgery (50.0% vs. 20.2%, HR 2.541 [1.119-5.770], p = 0.026). No significant association with age, sex, osteoporosis, scapholunate dissociation, step-off deformity, or intra-articular extension. CONCLUSION: Ulnar styloid osteolysis was observed in approximately one in six patients with distal radius fractures in this cohort; this finding was associated with multiple markers of fracture severity. KEY POINTS: Question How often does ulnar styloid osteolysis occur after a distal radius fracture without ulnar involvement, and what clinical factors are associated with its development? Findings Ulnar styloid osteolysis develops in up to 16.8% of patients with radial fractures not associated with ulnar fracture in our population. Clinical relevance Ulnar styloid osteolysis after radial fracture occurs more frequently in patients with greater fracture comminution, dorsal angulation, diastasis, and impaction, as well as smokers. It must be differentiated from inflammatory arthropathies to avoid unnecessary investigations.

articles.title: AI for reducing claims and compensation payments from missed fractures on radiographs.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the potential of BoneView, an artificial intelligence (AI) tool for fracture detection on radiographs in claims cases related to missed fractures that resulted in financial compensation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter study included all patients who submitted a claim and received financial compensation for missed fractures on radiographs between January 2013 and December 2019 across the 38 university hospitals of the Greater Paris area (AP-HP-France). For each claimant, 5 control patients were selected from a contemporary single-center cohort of patients who underwent radiographs of the same anatomical regions (with or without fracture) performed in the emergency department of a university hospital, irrespective of fracture status. Three radiologists (musculoskeletal fellow, 5-year fellowship-trained radiologist, and > 20-year expert) independently performed blinded, unassisted, and AI-assisted interpretations following a 3-month washout. Sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were calculated with and without AI and for standalone AI. Compensation amounts were used to estimate potentially avoidable payouts. RESULTS: 156 patients (mean age, 42.2 years; 113 (72.4%) males), including 26 claimants with missed fractures on radiographs and 130 controls, were evaluated. 27/130 (20.8%) of the control cohort had fractures. Standalone AI sensitivity was 80.8% (21/26; 95% CI [60.7-93.5]) for claimants and 96.3% (26/27; 95% CI [81.0-99.9]) for the control cohort (p = 0.10). AI assistance did not significantly improve sensitivity, with expert reader sensitivity increasing from 81.1% to 92.5% (p = 0.10). Total compensation was €282,850 (€10,878 per case). AI-assisted detection could have potentially mitigated €265,314, representing a 93.8% theoretical reduction in institutional financial liability. CONCLUSION: AI-assisted fracture detection identified most missed fractures on radiographs leading to compensation and may help reduce medicolegal risk and compensation-related financial burden. KEY POINTS: Question Can AI-assisted fracture detection identify fractures missed by radiologists on radiographs that led to compensated medicolegal claims and institutional financial liability? Findings Standalone AI detected 21/26 (80.8%) of missed fractures in patients with compensated claims, corresponding to €265,314/€282,850 (93.8%) of total compensation in this cohort. Clinical relevance AI-assisted fracture detection can potentially increase radiologists' diagnostic accuracy and reduce medicolegal risk and compensation-related financial burden. Implementing AI tools in emergency settings may significantly mitigate patient harm and institutional costs associated with missed fractures.

articles.title: Deep learning-based segmentation of the ischemic core and severe hypodensity on noncontrast head CT compared with CT perfusion and diffusion-weighted imaging.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the spatial overlap, imaging marker agreement, and outcome associations of acute ischemic regions of interest (ROIs) using deep-learning NCCT (DLNCCT) versus manual NCCT, CTP, and DWI-based segmentations. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We trained a deep learning model to segment ischemic ROIs on admission NCCT (DLNCCT). DLNCCT was compared with manual NCCT, CTP (rCBF < 30%/38%), and DWI using the Dice similarity coefficient (mean ± SD), Bland-Altman analysis (mean difference [95% CI]), and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). For each ROI, we compared NCCT imaging biomarkers: average lesion density (HU); modified net water uptake (mNWU in %); total volume (mL); and hypodense (≤ 26 HU) volume (mL). DLNCCT biomarkers were associated with reversed 90-day ordinal modified Rankin Scale (genOR [95% CI]). RESULTS: We used 218/762 train/test cases. Dice was 0.30 ± 0.30 between DLNCCT and manual segmentation, 0.22 ± 0.25 between DLNCCT-DWI, and 0.15 ± 0.22/0.21 ± 0.24 between CTP (rCBF < 30%/< 38%)-DWI. DLNCCT-DWI biomarker agreement was -1 HU (95% CI: -7; 6) for average density (CCC: 0.71), 4.9% (95% CI: -7.0; 16.8) for mNWU (CCC: 0.35), -16 mL (95% CI: -108; 76) for total volume (CCC: 0.57), and -4 mL (95% CI: -31; 23) for hypodense lesion volume (CCC: 0.75). Average lesion density (1.11 [95% CI: 1.06; 1.16]) and hypodense volume (0.85 [95% CI: 0.72; 0.99]) were associated with 90-day mRS. CONCLUSION: Spatial and biomarker agreement between DLNCCT and DWI was suboptimal but comparable to CTP-DWI. Nevertheless, DLNCCT-derived average lesion density and hypodense volume were associated with functional outcomes. KEY POINTS: Question Deep-learning models segment ischemic tissue on NCCT, but their spatial overlap and accuracy of imaging biomarker assessment relative to DWI and CTP core remain unclear. Findings Deep-learning NCCT segmentation showed good agreement with DWI in measuring hypodense (≤ 26 HU) volumes (- 4 mL [95% CI: -31; 23]; CCC 0.75). Clinical relevance Despite limited spatial overlap, NCCT-derived deep learning biomarkers showed agreement comparable to DWI, with improved performance in patients with poor ASPECTS and collateral scores. Hypodense volume and average lesion density were associated with functional outcome.

articles.title: Effects of CT-guided Radiofrequency Versus Microwave Ablation on Pulmonary Function in Individuals with Pulmonary Tumors: A Prospective Multicenter Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: Purpose To compare short-term changes in pulmonary function after radiofrequency ablation (RFA) versus microwave ablation (MWA) in participants being treated for pulmonary tumors. Materials and Methods This prospective, multicenter, randomized trial (Chinese Clinical Trial Registry no. ChiCTR2400079813) included participants who underwent CT-guided RFA or MWA between November 2023 and July 2024 at six institutions. Pulmonary function tests, including vital capacity, forced vital capacity, forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), percentage of predicted FEV1, maximum midexpiratory flow, and single-breath diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, were performed at baseline and 1 month after ablation. Secondary outcomes included procedure time, complications, and ablation completion rate. Intergroup comparisons and intragroup changes were analyzed. Results Overall, 138 participants with pulmonary tumors (mean age ± SD, 61.9 years ± 9.4; 72 female) were randomly assigned to undergo CT-guided RFA (n = 46) or MWA (n = 92). There was no evidence of a difference between the RFA and MWA groups for any pulmonary function parameter at baseline and at 1 month after ablation (eg, mean FEV1 for RFA vs MWA, 2.27 L ± 0.70 vs 2.26 L ± 0.64 at baseline [P = .92]; 2.24 L ± 0.60 vs 2.20 L ± 0.60 at 1 month [P = .77]), nor was there evidence of a difference in pulmonary function parameters within each group (eg, mean FEV1 with RFA, P = .32; mean FEV1 with MWA, P = .10). The mean procedure time was significantly shorter for MWA than for RFA (48.1 vs 61.4 minutes, respectively; P = .004). The rates of major complications were similar between the two groups (eg, pneumothorax requiring chest tube drainage [20% for MWA vs 26% for RFA; P = .38]). Complete ablation rates were high for both techniques (98% [90 of 92] for MWA vs 93% [43 of 46] for RFA; P = .33). Conclusion RFA and MWA demonstrated similar short-term influences on pulmonary function in participants with pulmonary tumors; however, MWA was associated with a shorter procedure time, with outcomes similar to those seen with RFA. Keywords: Interventional-Oncology, Pulmonary Tumor, Radiofrequency Ablation, Microwave Ablation, Pulmonary Function Supplemental material is available for this article. articles.title: Longitudinal MRI-based Delta-Habitat model for predicting pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate a machine learning model integrating habitat imaging features before and after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) to predict pathological complete response (pCR) to NACI in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). METHODS: A multicenter retrospective study was conducted involving 520 HNSCC patients who received NACI across three hospitals. Unlike conventional Delta-Radiomics, we developed Delta-Habitat model that integrates Pre-NACI and Post-NACI MRI spatial habitat radiomics features, and dynamically learns task-specific contributions from each timepoint. Predictive performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to quantify the contribution of individual features to model predictions. We assessed and compared the diagnostic performance of senior and junior radiologists, both with and without the aid of the Delta-Habitat model. RESULTS: Delta-Habitat model outperformed Pre-NACI feature-based models and traditional radiomics-based Delta-Rad model, with AUC of 0.828, 0.825 and 0.813 in validation and two external test cohorts respectively. Post-treatment neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (Post-NLR) was identified as an independent predictor of pCR. Integrating Delta-Radiomics and clinical features into Delta-Habitat model did not yield a significant improvement in predictive performance, the combined model showed slightly improved AUC over Delta-Habitat alone, reaching 0.877 (train), 0.834 (val), 0.837 (test1), and 0.834 (test2). SHAP analysis revealed that Post-NACI features contributed more substantially to model predictions than Pre-NACI features. The Delta-Habitat model consistently exhibited better performance than radiologists in comparative evaluations. Moreover, senior and junior radiologists both showed increases in AUC values with the assistance of the Delta-Habitat model, by 0.073 and 0.177 respectively on the internal validation cohort and by 0.087 and 0.142 on the external test cohort. CONCLUSIONS: The longitudinal MRI-based habitat model can provide valuable information for predicting the response to NACI in HNSCC and enhance radiologists' diagnostic performance.

articles.title: Injury mechanisms and imaging findings in mixed martial arts.
articles.abstract: Mixed martial arts (MMA) is a rapidly growing combat sport that combines striking and grappling disciplines including boxing, Muay Thai, karate, judo, and Brazilian jiu-jitsu (BJJ). As participation and professional competition increase, musculoskeletal radiologists become increasingly likely to encounter characteristic MMA-related injuries. Although craniofacial trauma, lacerations, and concussion remain the most common injuries in competition, several distinctive musculoskeletal injury patterns arise from grappling, takedowns, and submission techniques. Understanding the biomechanical forces generated by these manoeuvres contributes to accurate image interpretation and appropriate management. Injuries arising from submission techniques are particularly associated with recognisable imaging patterns. The arm bar most commonly results in ulnar collateral ligament injury at the elbow, whereas the Americana and Kimura shoulder locks may produce anterior and posterior capsulolabral injuries respectively. Heel hooks are associated with rotational knee trauma involving the anterior cruciate ligament and collateral ligaments, with injury patterns varying according to whether valgus-external rotation or varus-internal rotation forces are applied. Less common but highly characteristic injuries include combined lateral collateral ligament and anterolateral ligament injury with intact cruciate ligaments as a result of grappling guard positions and choke manoeuvres. This review summarises the major MMA techniques, associated mechanisms of injury, and key imaging findings relevant to musculoskeletal radiologists.

articles.title: Sports-related peripheral neuropathies in athletes: mechanisms, imaging evaluation, and sport-specific patterns.
articles.abstract: Peripheral neuropathy in athletes is increasingly recognized as a significant source of morbidity, with injury patterns varying according to the biomechanical demands of specific sports. Although peripheral nerve disorders in athletes may result from acute trauma, they more commonly arise from chronic, repetitive mechanical stress inherent to athletic activity. Despite their frequency, they frequently remain underdiagnosed, as clinical manifestations often overlap with other musculoskeletal disorders. Mechanisms of injury include compression, traction, laceration, ischemia, and repetitive microtrauma. Distinct athletic modalities are associated with characteristic neuropathies reflecting sport-specific kinematics and loading patterns. Awareness of these biomechanical factors and recognition of typical clinical presentations are essential for accurate assessment of athletes with suspected nerve injury. Diagnostic evaluation frequently requires advanced imaging modalities, particularly magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) and high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS), which enable detailed structural assessment of peripheral nerves and detection of secondary imaging findings. Electrodiagnostic studies may provide complementary functional information in selected cases. Early and precise diagnosis is critical to guide management, facilitate safe return to sport, and prevent long-term functional deficits. While most nerve disorders respond to conservative treatment, severe, progressive, or refractory cases may warrant surgical intervention to restore function and enable return to play (RTP). This review examines mechanisms of injury, clinical evaluation, classification systems, imaging findings, and sport-specific patterns of peripheral nerve injury across diverse athletic disciplines.

articles.title: Mastering the Art of Procedural Education in Radiology.
Preoperative Prediction of Lymph Node Metastasis in Rectal Cancer Using Multimodal Magnetic Resonance Imaging Radiomics Combined with Clinical Risk Factors.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate the preoperative predictive value of multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics combined with clinical risk factors for lymph node metastasis in rectal cancer, and to construct and validate an efficient and reproducible preoperative prediction model. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 129 patients with pathologically confirmed rectal cancer who underwent surgery at our hospital between 2017 and 2023. Preoperative pelvic T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging (T1CE), and complete clinical data were collected. Three-dimensional regions of interest were manually segmented on the tumors using ITK-SNAP software, and radiomic features were selected via variance filtering and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Patients were randomly divided into a training cohort (n = 90) and an internal validation cohort (n = 39) at a 7:3 ratio. Five Logistic regression prediction models were constructed: single-sequence radiomics, multimodal radiomics, multimodal radiomics combined with clinical risk factors, and clinical factors alone. Using postoperative pathology as the gold standard, the diagnostic performance of each model was evaluated by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. RESULTS: The multimodal radiomics combined with clinical risk factors model demonstrated the best predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.885 (95% CI: 0.819-0.937), sensitivity of 85.3%, specificity of 82.1%, and accuracy of 83.6% in the internal validation cohort. Its performance was significantly superior to that of the single-sequence models, the multimodal radiomics model, and the clinical model alone (all P < 0.05). Entropy from T2WI, peak enhancement from T1CE, tumor volume, tumor size, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) were identified as independent predictors of lymph node metastasis. Calibration curves and decision curve analysis confirmed that the model was well-calibrated and provided substantial net clinical benefit. CONCLUSION: Integrating multimodal MRI radiomics from T2WI and T1CE with clinical indicators such as CEA and NLR significantly improves the preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis in rectal cancer, demonstrating promising clinical applicability. However, as this was a single-center retrospective study, further multicenter, large-sample external validation is warranted to confirm the stability and generalizability of the model.

articles.title: Is the First Pass Effect Really a First Pass Epiphenomenon?
Venous Outflow Imaging in Acute Ischemic Stroke: An ASFNR State of Practice.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Venous outflow (VO) imaging describes the egress limb of the cerebral collateral circulation and has been associated with outcome in acute ischemic stroke; its added value beyond arterial collaterals and perfusion measures remains uncertain. More than a dozen VO measures have been proposed on CT and MR techniques used in acute stroke, spanning three physical signals: venous opacification, venous transit and venous oxygenation. They differ in what they measure, in evidence maturity and in readiness for reporting. METHODS: A writing group reviewed the peer-reviewed studies of cerebral venous drainage measures in acute ischemic stroke. The scope is CT and MRI obtained during routine acute stroke evaluation, excluding measures that require catheter angiography or ultrasound. We describe each measure's acquisition, definition, evidence and technical limitations, and propose a reporting framework based on these features. KEY MESSAGE: VO markers are descriptive prognostic measures, not treatment-selection criteria. The cortical vein opacification score (COVES) has the most mature CTA evidence and may be considered when venous timing is adequate, though meta-analyses support an association rather than a threshold; comprehensive venous outflow (CVO) adds the internal cerebral vein. Prolonged venous transit (PVT) adds a temporal dimension read from perfusion, but remains investigational, as do the composite arterial-venous scores, quantitative venous timing and oxygen extraction fraction mapping. Susceptibility signs index deoxygenation and venous blood volume, not drainage. Reporting should name the technique and describe opacification, transit or oxygenation findings in their own terms. The evidence base is predominantly anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion imaged before thrombectomy.

articles.title: Axial versus Axial-Plus-Coronal DWI for Brainstem Infarct Detection: A Blinded Multi-reader Multi-case Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute brainstem infarcts are difficult to detect because of their small size, susceptibility artifacts, and low lesion conspicuity. Although coronal diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) has been proposed to improve detection, its incremental value beyond standard axial DWI remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether adding coronal DWI improves diagnostic performance, reader confidence, and recognition of diagnostically challenging acute brainstem infarcts. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective counterbalanced multi-reader multi-case study included 100 brain MRIs (50 with and 50 without acute brainstem infarction) performed 2022-2026. Six readers (three fellowship-trained neuroradiologists and three neuroradiology fellows) independently interpreted examinations using either axial DWI alone or axial-plus-coronal DWI. Positive cases were confirmed by consensus review of imaging findings and clinical records. Primary outcomes were sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. Secondary outcomes included reader confidence, identification of cases in which coronal DWI was considered particularly helpful (or desired if unavailable), and subgroup analyses by lesion characteristics and reader experience. RESULTS: Accuracy was similar for axial-only and axial-plus-coronal DWI (93.3% [95% CI 89.9-95.6] vs 93.0% [89.5-95.4], p=.84), as were sensitivity (87.9% [81.7-92.2] vs 89.3% [CI 83.4-93.3], p=.65) and specificity (98.7% [95.2-99.6] vs 96.6%, [92.4-98.6], p=.24). Attendings demonstrated improved sensitivity with coronal DWI (83.8% [73.8-90.5] to 92.0% [83.6-96.3]);fellows showed no consistent benefit. For infarcts ≤5 mm, sensitivity was 73.0% with axial DWI and 82.5% with axial-plus-coronal DWI (OR, 2.27, 0.79-6.51; p=.13). Confidence was higher with coronal DWI (Δ=0.18, 0.07-0.29; p=0.002). Coronal DWI was flagged as helpful more frequently for positive than negative cases (39.3% vs. 14.4%, OR 3.85, 2.00-7.43), and axial-phase readers more often desired coronal DWI when their interpretation was incorrect (46.2% vs. 17.2%, OR 4.1, 1.03-16.5). CONCLUSIONS: Adding coronal DWI did not significantly improve overall diagnostic performance for acute brainstem infarction in this multi-reader study but significantly increased reader confidence and aided recognition of diagnostically challenging examinations. Subgroup analyses suggested possible benefit for small infarcts. CLINICAL IMPACT: Coronal DWI may be most valuable as a complementary sequence that reduces diagnostic uncertainty and supports interpretation of subtle brainstem infarcts rather than increasing overall detection accuracy.

articles.title: An approximation of MRI R2* as a rapid surrogate of nigral iron in Parkinson's disease.
articles.abstract: Nigral iron accumulation is a robust imaging marker of Parkinson's disease and is commonly assessed using R2* mapping. However, its clinical implementation is limited by long acquisition times. An alternative metric, effective R2, derived from dual-contrast proton density- and T2-weighted MRI, has recently been proposed as a fast surrogate of tissue iron content. Using data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), we evaluated the diagnostic and longitudinal performance of effective R2 in the substantia nigra (SN) across multiple scanner platforms. Cross-sectional analysis demonstrated significantly higher effective R2 values in de novo Parkinson's disease patients (n=187) compared with prodromal subjects (n=26), with consistent effects across acquisition protocols. In Siemens data (177 patients and 25 prodromal subjects), effective R2 achieved good discriminative performance for Parkinson's disease classification (AUC = 0.85). Longitudinal analysis for 14 patients over 36 months showed no significant change in effective R2 values despite clinical progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III scores. These findings indicate that effective R2 provides robust cross-sectional discrimination of early Parkinson's disease but with limited sensitivity to disease progression.

articles.title: Short-Video Experience and Brain-State Dynamics During the Processing of Rapidly Changing Video Information in Youth.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Short-video platforms frequently expose youth to rapidly changing video information. Processing such inputs requires large-scale brain networks to reorganize with the ongoing context. However, little is known about these dynamics or their association with prior short-video viewing experience. METHODS: A total of 108 youth aged 8-18 years completed resting-state and naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI scans. The movie comprised rapidly changing and relatively continuous segments. Hidden Markov models were applied to 17 cortical networks to identify recurrent brain states, and a joint rest-task analysis examined the context specificity of the main finding. RESULTS: Eight task-related brain states were identified. Five differed in fractional occupancy (FO) between conditions, and global switching was slightly higher during rapidly changing segments. State 7 was the only state showing an interaction with short-video viewing experience. Its FO was higher during relatively continuous than rapidly changing segments among participants reporting no prior Douyin use, whereas the condition difference was not significant among those reporting prior Douyin use. Visit frequency analyses showed a similar pattern. The interaction remained robust after covariate adjustment and was also observed in the joint rest-task analysis, with no significant group difference at rest. CONCLUSIONS: Rapidly changing video information was associated with brain-state reorganization in youth. Douyin use was associated with lower State 7 occupancy during relatively continuous narrative segments; no significant group difference in the matched state's occupancy was detected at rest. These findings provide new evidence linking short-video viewing experience to context-dependent brain dynamics in youth.

articles.title: Working memory supports cognitive control by orchestrating dimension-specific modulation during late conflict resolution.
articles.abstract: Working memory plays a central role in cognitive control, yet how it shapes target- and distractor-related processing over time remains unclear. Here, we combined a working memory load manipulation with a modified Stroop task in which distractors preceded targets. Behaviorally, we found that pre-exposure to the distractor eliminated the congruency effect, but this benefit was absent under high load. This pattern suggests that the benefit of advance distractor presentation is sensitive to concurrent working-memory demands. Electrophysiologically, the distractor-locked lateralized readiness potential (LRP) indicated that working-memory load altered distractor-related response activation before target onset. After target onset, load-related modulation emerged during late conflict resolution, as indexed by the sustained potential (SP), whereas earlier intervals associated with attentional selection (posterior N2) and conflict monitoring (N450) did not show load-dependent modulation. Time-frequency decoding and representational similarity analysis further revealed distinct spectro-temporal profiles of target- and distractor-related processing: target-related coding emerged earlier in the theta band (540-780 ms), consistent with stimulus-response mapping, whereas distractor-related coding emerged later in the mu-beta band (870-1180 ms), consistent with response-related regulation. These findings highlight dimension- and stage-specific patterns of working-memory modulation during conflict resolution.

articles.title: AngioSeg: Automated Hepatic Angiosome Segmentation on Cone-Beam CT for Yttrium-90 Radioembolization Dosimetry.
articles.abstract: Accurate dosimetry planning in Yttrium-90 (Y-90) radioembolization (SIRT) requires accurate estimation of the tissue volume receiving microsphere deposition. The angiosome, defined as the tissue territory perfused by a selected feeding artery, serves as a practical patient-specific surrogate for this volume. However, acquiring true angiosome volume requires manual segmentation of cone-beam CT (CBCT), which is impractical intraoperatively. Thus, the present study trained a self-configuring nnU-Net (AngioSeg) to automate angiosome segmentation. Fifty CBCT scans were manually annotated and validated across 2D, 3D full-resolution, and ensemble configurations, assessed by Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, and volume agreement. The 3D model performed best, with a mean DSC of 0.88 and a median HD95 of 4.18 mm, achieving non-inferiority to human inter-rater agreement. The mean absolute volume difference was 6.10 mL. AngioSeg segments the angiosome at the level of a human rater, supporting eventual personalized intraoperative dosimetry in Y-90 radioembolization.

articles.title: MRI-guided HDR brachytherapy or integrated VMAT boost for tumour-targeted dose escalation in localised prostate cancer: long-term results of the TARGET study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate local control of the gross tumour volume in localised prostate cancer following focal dose escalation delivered by integrated boost volumetric modulated arc therapy (IB-VMAT) or high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients with localised prostate cancer and an intraprostatic lesion identified on multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) were included in a prospective, non-randomised phase II study. Eighty patients received VMAT to the prostate 76 Gy/38 fractions. Boost strategy involved an IB of 95 Gy/38 fractions (IB-VMAT) or a single fraction of 10 Gy (HDR-VMAT). Three patients received 6 months androgen deprivation therapy. The primary endpoint was 3-year local control (LC) assessed by MRI or MRI-guided biopsy. Secondary outcomes included biochemical failure-free survival (bFFS), toxicity and health-related quality of life (HRQoL), assessed using CTCAE v.4.0, the American Urological Association Symptom Score and EPIC. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 4.8 years (IQR, 4.0-8.0). Sixty-six patients underwent a 3-year MRI or MRI-guided biopsy; one patient demonstrated recurrence within the boost volume. Four patients demonstrated intraprostatic failure outside the boost volume and three patients developed regional/distant metastases. Eight patients experienced biochemical failure (4 IB-VMAT; 4 HDR-VMAT). Overall, 5-year bFFS was 86.9% (95% CI, 79.1-95.5). No substantial differences in late toxicities and HRQoL were observed between cohorts. CONCLUSION: Intraprostatic tumour-targeted dose escalation using IB-VMAT or HDR-VMAT provided high rates of LC and bFFS with limited adverse impact in late toxicity and HRQoL. Randomised studies are needed to further define the merits and differences between the two techniques.

articles.title: A Rare Case of Arterial Tortuosity Syndrome: Serial Prenatal Ultrasound Findings in the Second and Third Trimesters.
The Coffee Bean Gallbladder Sign in Acute Hepatitis: A CEUS Imaging Case Report.
Segmentation-perturbation propagation in pretrained foundation-model embeddings versus IBSI-aligned radiomics for radiologist-assessed lung-nodule malignancy classification on the LIDC-IDRI cohort.
articles.abstract: Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort.Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics.Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone.&#xD.

articles.title: Quantifying multi-lesion detection and localization in whole-body FDG PET/CT with a multimodal foundation model.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop a 3D AI framework for detecting and localizing multiple lesions in whole-body FDG PET/CT, and to evaluate whether a pretrained PET/CT foundation model can improve lesion detection performance compared with conventional training from scratch.ApproachThe AutoPET cohort comprised 1,014 studies divided into 700 training, 114 validation, and 200 subject-independent test studies. Tumor masks were converted into 3D bounding boxes. We developed a one-stage 3D lesion detector using a PlainConvUNet backbone to extract multi-scale encoder-decoder features for lesion classification and box regression. To leverage foundation-model representations, the PlainConvUNet backbone was initialized with weights from our previously developed multi-center PET/CT foundation model, pretrained using masked autoencoding, and subsequently fine-tuned for lesion detection. Four configurations were compared: PET+CT trained from scratch, PET only, CT only, and PET+CT initialized from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model. Detection performance was evaluated using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) and alternative FROC (AFROC) analyses, qualitative analysis, and lesion-size-stratified operating curves.Main resultsMultimodal PET+CT consistently outperformed either modality alone across task-based detection metrics, demonstrating the complementary contributions of metabolic and anatomical information. Importantly, initialization from the pretrained PET/CT foundation model further enhanced lesion detection performance compared with training the same PET+CT detector from scratch, increasing absolute FROC sensitivity by 0.034-0.041 across the evaluated 1-4 false-positive-per-scan operating range and improving AFROC AUC by 0.028. Detection performance increased with lesion size, with small lesions remaining the most challenging. The separation between the pretrained and randomly initialized PET+CT configurations was more evident in the smaller-lesion strata, whereas their operating curves increasingly overlapped for larger lesions.SignificanceThis study provides a detection-centered, task-based characterization of multi-lesion analysis in whole-body PET/CT. Multimodal PET+CT improves lesion detection compared with either modality alone, lesion size is a major determinant of detection performance, and initialization from a pretrained PET/CT foundation model provides an additional performance improvement.

articles.title: Experimental verification of clinical dose and LET maps for LET-informed proton therapy.
articles.abstract: Objective:Linear energy transfer (LET)-informed proton therapy has the potential to improve biological treatment planning beyond the conventional, constant-RBE assumption. Its clinical translation, however, requires experimental tools capable of verifying spatially resolved dose and dose-averaged LET (LETD) distributions under clinically relevant conditions. We recently introduced an optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) film-based detector system that simultaneously measures two-dimensional (2D) absorbed dose and LETD. This work provides a first assessment of the system for verifying dose and LETDdistributions from clinical proton therapy plans.Approach:The system was tested at two proton therapy centers, ranging from simple uniform fields to more complex geometries, including Bragg curve measurements and a clinically realistic anthropomorphic head phantom treatment plan. Measured dose and LETDdistributions were compared against commercial treatment planning system (TPS) calculations and, for selected fields, to external Monte Carlo particle transport simulations due to the absence of traceability of LETD. For non-uniform irradiations, agreement was assessed using gamma analysis with 3%/2 mm and 5%/2 mm criteria for dose and LETD, respectively.Main results:For uniform fields, measured dose and LETDdistributions generally agreed with TPS and independent Monte Carlo simulations across a range of clinically relevant irradiation conditions. In the Bragg curve measurement, gamma pass rates were 96.6% for dose and 99.7% for LETD, with the largest dose discrepancy observed near the Bragg peak, consistent with a current over-correction of detector quenching in high-LET regions to be improved in future work. In the anthropomorphic phantom, gamma pass rates ranged from 75% to 100% for dose and from 45% to 95% for LETD, with a single layer showing a sub-50% pass rate for LETD. Failing regions were confined to high-dose superior layers for dose and distal-edge, high-LET regions for LETD.Significance:The presented results support the detector system's use as an experimental benchmarking tool for TPS-calculated dose and LETDmaps. Given this and the system's ability to simultaneously measure 2D dose and LETDmaps with high spatial resolution and minimal field perturbation, the system shows promise for future commissioning workflows for LET-informed proton therapy.

articles.title: Review of radiobiological dose rate effects at the edge between conventional and FLASH.
articles.abstract: The shift from passive scattering to active pencil beam scanning (PBS) in proton therapy, alongside techniques such as flattening filter-free photon therapy, has increased dose rates in clinical radiotherapy from <0.4 Gy/s to 0.4-35 Gy/s. Meanwhile, ultra-high dose rate radiotherapy (FLASH, ≥40 Gy/s) has emerged as a novel modality that spares normal tissue while maintaining tumor control. Yet, dose rate effects within the 0.4-35 Gy/s range have traditionally been considered negligible. Recent reports of unexpected necroses after proton PBS irradiations challenge this assumption, prompting a reevaluation of potential dose-rate-dependent effects in this intermediate range.This review summarizes current evidence on dose rate effects within 0.4-35 Gy/s, derived from in vivo models (including zebrafish embryos and rodents), in-vitro experiments and water radiolysis studies. Selected experimental and retrospective observations suggest that dose rates in this intermediate range may modify the biological response and, under certain conditions, increase toxicity relative to conventional reference dose rates (<0.4 Gy/s). The magnitude and even direction of dose rate effects appear to depend on radiation quality, total dose, temporal delivery structure, oxygenation, linear energy transfer, tissue type and biological endpoint. The observations described in this review are hypothesis-generating rather than threshold-defining, highlighting the need for further investigation in experimental conditions, preclinical models, and clinical settings.

articles.title: Pulse-width-specific phase space modeling and reference beam characterization for UHDR electron LINAC in FLASH-RT.
articles.abstract: FLASH radiotherapy requires ultra-high dose rates (>40 Gy/s), yet commercial treatment planning systems are currently unavailable. Monte Carlo (MC) simulation offers high transport accuracy, but full-head modeling for every setup is computationally prohibitive. This work establishes a methodology for generating pulse-width-specific phase-space files for the Mobetron UHDR (9 MeV), accounting for systematic beam quality shifts caused by RF waveguide loading across pulse widths of 1.2-4.0 μs. Approach: Using GAMOS 6.2.0 MC simulations, voxelized dose distributions were post-processed via an iterative script to refine source-level parameters against experimental targets. Mean energy was optimized by matching phantom-measured R50, while energy spread was refined using surface dose and build-up gradients. Relationships derived from a mid-range 6 cm applicator were applied across clinical apertures (2.5-10 cm) to test aperture-independence. The geometric mean of experimental pulse widths (2.28 μs) was evaluated as a single reference condition. Main Results: Phase space files were generated across pulse widths and apertures. For the A6I6 reference, mean energy decreased monotonically from 9.58±0.24 to 9.04±0.24 MeV with pulse width, best described by a logarithmic model (LOO-RMSE=0.033 MeV). Energy spread increased linearly from 0.173±0.020 to 0.287±0.020 MeV (LOO-RMSE=0.005 MeV). Cross-aperture validation confirmed these shifts occur upstream of collimation. Evaluating the 2.28 μs reference predicted 9.30 MeV mean energy and 0.215 MeV energy spread, yielding depth-dose deviations ≤1.3 mm across experimental extremes and satisfying AAPM TG-106 tolerances (≤2.0 mm). Significance: This work provides pulse-width-specific phase-space characterization for Mobetron FLASH commissioning. Cross-validated regression models enable beam parameter prediction within 1.2-4.0 μs, and the 2.28 μs reference phase space streamlines routine planning while maintaining clinical accuracy.&#xD.

articles.title: Diffusion-weighted MRI-derived μDiff index and extracellular volume fraction for severity classification of acute pancreatitis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)-derived quantitative index (μDiff) and T1 mapping-derived extracellular volume (ECV) fraction for distinguishing mild acute pancreatitis (AP) from the combined moderately severe or severe category, and to compare their discrimination with magnetic resonance severity index (MRSI) and clinical scores. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled patients with AP who underwent abdominal MRI early after admission between 2024 and 2025. MRI protocols included conventional imaging, DWI, and pre- and postcontrast T1 mapping. The DWI-derived μDiff index was calculated from signal intensities at b values of 200 and 1500 s/mm2, whereas ECV was derived from pancreatic and blood-pool T1 values. AP severity was classified according to the 2012 revised Atlanta classification. Five single-predictor and four two-predictor logistic models were evaluated using AUCs with 95% confidence intervals, paired DeLong comparisons, and 2,000-resample bootstrap internal validation; calibration and exploratory decision-curve analyses were also performed. RESULTS: Among 140 patients with AP, 99 had mild AP and 41 had moderately severe or severe AP. Both μDiff and ECV increased with severity. μDiff showed an AUC of 0.896 (95% CI, 0.836-0.956), with no statistically significant difference from MRSI (0.878; 95% CI, 0.811-0.946; DeLong p = 0.720). The μDiff + MRSI model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.972 (95% CI, 0.948-0.996) and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.969, with improved discrimination over μDiff and MRSI alone (Holm-adjusted p = 0.019 and p = 0.003, respectively). Its corrected calibration slope and Brier score were 0.911 and 0.067. CONCLUSIONS: The DWI-derived μDiff index showed good discrimination of Atlanta-defined AP severity, with performance statistically comparable to MRSI. Their combination improved discrimination and retained high performance after internal validation, supporting their complementary value for severity classification.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI for Parkinson Disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Objective: The diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains challenging due to clinical overlap with other parkinsonian syndromes and the absence of widely available imaging biomarkers. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) enables in vivo visualization of neuromelanin in the substantia nigra (SN) and locus coeruleus (LC), where signal loss reflects dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the SN and noradrenergic neurodegeneration in the LC. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in differentiating PD from healthy controls. MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 2025. Studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of NM-MRI in PD versus healthy controls were included. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed methodological quality using QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a random-effects bivariate model, with construction of a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Subgroup analyses were performed by anatomical region (SN, LC) and imaging parameter (volume, area, signal intensity, contrast ratio, subjective assessment), along with meta-regression and Deeks' funnel plot for publication bias. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251088071). RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies comprising 2,268 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.0 % (95 % CI, 85.3-90.2 %) and 84.4 % (95 % CI, 80.6-87.5 %), respectively, with an area under the SROC curve of 0.901 and low heterogeneity (I2 = 3.6 % for sensitivity, 9.2 % for specificity). Volumetric analysis of the SN yielded robust and reproducible performance (sensitivity 88.0 %, specificity 85.5 %), while subjective visual assessment achieved the highest sensitivity (90.8 %) but lower reproducibility. Meta-regression identified no significant effect of MRI acquisition parameters on diagnostic accuracy, and no significant publication bias was detected. CONCLUSION: NM-MRI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for differentiating PD from healthy controls, with volumetric analysis of the substantia nigra offering a robust and reproducible imaging biomarker. As the included studies compared PD with healthy controls rather than with other parkinsonian syndromes, these findings should not yet be extrapolated to the differential diagnosis of PD from other forms of parkinsonism.

articles.title: MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram for differentiating FIGO 2023 stage I from stage II-IV endometrial cancer: a multicenter study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Preoperative identification of FIGO 2023 stage I endometrial cancer (EC) is important for treatment planning. We aimed to develop and validate a deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) based on multiparametric MRI to distinguish stage I EC from stage II-IV disease. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This study retrospectively enrolled patients from three centers. Patients from Centers 1 and 2 were randomly split into a training set (n = 616), and an internal test set (n = 158), and Center 3 served as an external test set (n = 232). The DLRN integrated deep-learning features, intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics features, and clinical characteristics. The DLRN was compared with clinical, radiomics, and deep-learning models. Discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with AUCs compared using DeLong's test. RESULTS: A total of 1006 patients (mean age, 56.5 ± 9.7 years) were analyzed. In the internal test set, the DLRN achieved an AUC of 0.852, higher than the clinical (0.673; p = 0.001), original radiomics (0.765; p = 0.030), and combined radiomics (0.793; p = 0.050) models. In the external test set, the DLRN remained robust (AUC = 0.829) and outperformed the clinical, original radiomics, and combined radiomics models (AUC = 0.680, 0.681, and 0.743; all p < 0.005). With DLRN assistance, radiologists showed improved diagnostic performance. CONCLUSION: The MRI-based DLRN showed robust discrimination between FIGO 2023 stage I and stage II-IV EC across test sets, supporting its potential for preoperative risk stratification and decision support. KEY POINTS: Question The introduction of the FIGO 2023 staging system has made the differentiation between stages more challenging, highlighting the need for better tools. Findings A new MRI-based deep-learning radiomics nomogram (DLRN) accurately identifies high-risk patients, significantly outperforming traditional and individual clinical prediction methods. Critical relevance statement This tool helps doctors make better preoperative treatment plans, potentially improving patient outcomes in endometrial cancer.

articles.title: Peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations in the 2025 ISSVA classification: a practical MRI approach.
articles.abstract: The 2025 update of the International Society for the Study of Vascular Anomalies (ISSVA) classification introduced several imaging-relevant changes, including the recognition of potentially unique vascular anomalies. Although the main framework for vascular tumors remains unchanged, with continued subdivision into benign, borderline, and malignant tumors, the most radiologically relevant structural changes concern vascular malformations, which were reorganized into fast-flow lesions, slow-flow lesions, and developmental anomalies of named vessels. These updates are important for radiologists because imaging plays a central role in assessing hemodynamic characteristics, defining lesion extent, and identifying findings relevant to procedural planning and multidisciplinary management. This educational review presents an author-derived four-step framework that organizes established MRI observations for peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations according to the structure and terminology of the 2025 ISSVA classification, including hemodynamic assessment, vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy. KEY POINTS: Question Imaging-relevant organizational and terminology changes in the 2025 ISSVA classification require practical guidance for consistent MRI assessment and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations. Findings An author-derived four-step, flow-based framework organizes hemodynamics, dominant vascular components, tissue composition, lesion extent, and treatment-relevant anatomy into structured MRI assessment. Critical relevance statement The MRI-focused framework provides a practical way to apply the 2025 ISSVA classification consistently in image interpretation, terminology, and reporting of peripheral and soft-tissue vascular malformations.

articles.title: Projection restoration with dual-domain Swin refinement for sparse-view CT reconstruction.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: We investigated whether projection restoration before reconstruction, followed by image-domain refinement, improves sparse-view computed tomography (CT) quality under aggressive undersampling. METHODS: A compact dual-domain Swin framework restores sparse sinograms before geometry-aware differentiable filtered back projection (FBP) and refines the resulting images. The projection branch uses gated Swin processing and angular upsampling with a bicubic bypass. Abdominal AAPM sinograms contained 2304 full views, retaining 576, 288, and 144 views at 4x, 8x, and 16x. Comparators were FBP, bilinear and bicubic interpolation, ProCT, and geometry-adapted DuDoTrans; ablations used ten epochs. RESULTS: DuDoSwin achieved PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS of 45.64 dB/0.981/0.011 at 4x, 44.11 dB/0.975/0.020 at 8x, and 42.02 dB/0.963/0.035 at 16x. Mean PSNR and SSIM exceeded ProCT and DuDoTrans; DuDoTrans had lower LPIPS at 4x and 8x. DuDoSwin used 1.36-1.80 million parameters but was slower than both learned comparators. Comparisons against interpolation and DuDoTrans were significant in Holm-corrected paired tests. Bypass removal improved ablation PSNR by 0.35 dB at 8x. Evaluation included the validation patient; exclusion changed mean PSNR by at most 0.1 dB and altered no ranking. Slice-wise tests ignore within-patient dependence. CONCLUSION: Explicit projection restoration followed by image-domain refinement yielded favorable PSNR and SSIM, with perceptual metric and computational trade-offs. Neither residual shortcut improved the 8x ablation results. Independent patient evaluation remains necessary.
articles.journal: Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg

articles.title: RadStructAgent: agentic structuring of free-text chest X-ray reports with small language models.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Variability in chest X-ray (CXR) reporting hinders training and evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) for radiology report generation. Our previous study showed that Structured Radiology Report Generation (SRRG)-style supervision improves VLM-based CXR reporting over free-text supervision. Here, we examine this finding in a larger multi-institutional setting and address a key preprocessing challenge: reliable free-text-to-structured-report conversion using open-source small language models (SLMs). METHODS: We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-3B using free-text and SRRG-style structured supervision across 10 institutions covering 97K samples. We then propose RadStructAgent, an agentic framework that converts free-text CXR reports into structured reports using SLMs, combining LLM-based orchestration, judge feedback, and feedback-guided revision. RadStructAgent is evaluated on 1,000 free-text CXR reports using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. RESULTS: For the report generation task, structured supervision improves Qwen2.5-VL-3B over free-text supervision, increasing GREEN from 0.494 to 0.539, with similar gains across other clinical metrics. For the structuring task, RadStructAgent improves both clinical quality (GREEN) and anatomy-level assignment (RadFAA): for Qwen3-4B, from 0.844 to 0.867 and 0.883 to 0.891; for Qwen3-8B, from 0.863 to 0.881 and 0.889 to 0.902. CONCLUSION: Structured supervision remains effective for VLM-based CXR report generation when evaluated in a larger multi-institutional setting. RadStructAgent shows that open-source SLMs can be strengthened through agentic verification and refinement, providing a resource-efficient approach for offline and privacy-preserving structured report preparation. Our code, prompt templates, and configuration files are publicly available at: https://github.com/badhon1512/RadStructAgent .
articles.journal: Int J Comput Assist Radiol Surg

articles.title: Safety and efficacy of endovascular treatment of wide-neck intracranial aneurysms: comparison between stent-assisted coiling and intrasaccular flow disruption with the contour device.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the association between endovascular treatment strategy and the occurrence of postprocedural DWI lesions and periprocedural complications as well as retreatment rates in patients undergoing elective endovascular treatment (EVT) for unruptured wide-neck intracranial aneurysms. METHODS: This retrospective single-center study includes all consecutive patients who underwent elective EVT with stent-assisted coiling (SAC) or Contour device (CD) of unruptured wide-neck intracranial aneurysms between January 2019 and January 2026. Wide-neck aneurysms were defined as aneurysms with a neck ≥4 mm and/or a dome-to-neck ratio < 2. Postprocedural MRI was assessed for new DWI lesions. Uni- and multivariable regression analysis was performed to identify predictors for the primary outcome variables DWI lesions and periprocedural complications. Secondary outcome variables included procedure time, residual perfusion and retreatment rates. RESULTS: A total of 96 patients (50% SAC, 50% CD) were included. Postprocedural DWI lesions were detected in 60% of patients overall with a significant difference between the two groups (78% SAC vs. 43% CD; p<0.001). Periprocedural complications (SAC 13% vs. CD 13%; p = 1.0) and retreatment rates (SAC 7% vs. CD 6%; p = 0.754) did not differ between the two groups. In a multivariate regression analysis, SAC (aOR 4.15, 95% CI 1.39-12.4, p = 0.011) was an independent predictor of postprocedural DWI lesions. CONCLUSION: In elective EVT of unruptured wide-neck intracranial aneurysms, stent-assisted coiling was associated with a significantly higher rate of postprocedural DWI lesions compared to the Contour device. Periprocedural complications and retreatment rates were similar between the treatment strategies.

articles.title: Multifocal Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen-avid Cholangiocarcinoma Mimicking Prostate Cancer Metastases.
Assessing microvascular heterogeneity in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and peritumoral tissue using DCE-MRI pharmacokinetic parameters.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop DCE-MRI parameters based logistic regression models to evaluate microvascular heterogeneity between esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and cephalic peritumoral esophageal segmental tissues. METHODS: 133 consecutive ESCC patients receiving preoperative DCE-MRI from two centers were randomly divided into the training, internal validation and external validation cohorts at a ratio of 8:2:2. Mean, standard deviation (SD), coefficient of variation (CV) of DCE-MRI derived reflux rate (Kep), endothelial transfer constant (Ktrans) and fractional extravascular extracellular space volume (Ve) were compared between tumor (T) and five cephalic peritumoral esophageal segmental tissues at incremental 1-5 cm (recorded as PT1-PT5), and the statistical differential parameters were selected to develop logistic regression models to improve assessment of microvascular heterogeneity between ESCC and cephalic peritumoral esophageal segmental tissues. Model's performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with DeLong's test. RESULTS: All parameters showed differences among T, PT1, PT2 and PT3 except among PT3-PT5. Ve_CV and Kep_mean showed discriminatory ability among T, PT1, PT2 and PT3-5 (P-values < 0.05). Multivariate models by combining Ve_CV and Kep_mean outperformed Ve_CV or Kep_mean to show microvascular heterogeneity in T vs. PT2 (model AUC: 0.830, 0.917, and 0.818), and in T vs. PT3-5 (model AUC: 0.921, 0.845, and 0.857), while Ve_CV outperformed model for T vs. PT1 or Kep_mean (Ve_CV AUC: 0.716, 0.872, and 0.787) in the training, internal and external validation cohorts, respectively (P-values < 0.05). CONCLUSION: Our multivariate models help discriminate ESCC vs. PT2 or PT3-5 whereas Ve_CV can discriminate ESCC vs. PT1. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: In this study on DCE-MRI, after consolidating peritumoral tissues with 3-5 cm from the cephalic tumor margin of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma into a single group due to no significant differences among them, significant differences were identified among the tumor, peritumoral tissues 1 cm, 2 cm, and 3-5 cm from the margin, reflecting progressive microvascular heterogeneity with the incremental distances. Model by combination of mean reflux rate and coefficient of variation of fractional extravascular extracellular space volume (Ve_CV) help discriminate microvascular heterogeneity between tumor and cephalic peritumoral tissues except that Ve_CV help discriminate tumor vs. 1 cm from the tumor margin.

articles.title: Fetal Liver Volume and Morphology in Growth-Restricted Fetuses and Their Association With Neonatal Morbidity: An MRI Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) may induce redistribution of the fetal circulation to preserve perfusion of vital organs. Reduced hepatic delivery of oxygen- and nutrient-rich blood may cause volumetric and morphological remodeling. PURPOSE: To quantify fetal liver volume and morphology in FGR and assess associations with adverse neonatal outcomes. STUDY TYPE: Single-center, prospective and retrospective. POPULATION: Ninety-two singleton pregnancies: 36 FGR cases (prospective) and 56 appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) controls (retrospective). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3-T, True Fast Imaging with Steady-State Free Precession (TrueFISP) for fetal liver and body imaging, and TrueFISP or Half-Fourier Acquisition Single-shot Turbo Spin-Echo for brain imaging. ASSESSMENT: The fetal liver, body, and brain were segmented using deep learning tools. Liver volume, liver-to-body and brain-to-liver volume ratios, and 12 liver PyRadiomics shape features were assessed. Neonates were followed for composite adverse neonatal outcomes (CANO) until discharge. STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear regression assessed associations with gestational age in AGA fetuses. Linear mixed-effects models compared groups, adjusting for gestational age and fetal sex. Univariable logistic regression assessed associations with CANO. Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate at 0.05. RESULTS: FGR fetuses had significantly lower liver volume than AGA fetuses (74.95 ± 1.76 vs. 114.89 ± 2.18 cm3), lower liver-to-body ratio (0.053 ± 0.001 vs. 0.057 ± 0.001), and higher brain-to-liver ratio (2.637 ± 0.085 vs. 1.978 ± 0.047). FGR fetuses demonstrated significantly less elongated liver geometry, (10.7% higher PyRadiomics elongation values) and had a significantly higher surface-to-volume ratio (11.9%). CANO occurred in 30/92 neonates (27 FGR, 3 AGA). Higher brain-to-liver ratio (OR = 4.12, 95% CI: 1.93-8.77), PyRadiomics elongation values (less elongated geometry; OR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.26-3.30), PyRadiomics flatness values (less flattened geometry; OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07-2.65), and surface-to-volume ratio (OR = 3.26, 95% CI: 1.80-5.90) were significantly associated with CANO. DATA CONCLUSION: FGR was associated with reduced fetal liver size and altered geometry, which were associated with neonatal morbidity. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: 2.

articles.title: Cervicocerebral angiography in trauma using split-bolus whole-body CT - comparison with dedicated neuroradiological CT angiography.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine whether split-bolus whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) provides sufficient cervicocerebral arterial opacification and diagnostic evaluability for vascular assessment in polytrauma compared with dedicated neuroradiological computed tomography angiography (CTA). METHODS: In this retrospective single-centre study, 130 polytrauma patients undergoing split-bolus WBCT were age- and sex-matched to 130 patients undergoing dedicated head-and-neck CTA between January 2023 and June 2025. Arterial attenuation was measured in 15 cervicocerebral segments. Adequate vessel opacification was defined as ≥ 250 HU. Five radiologists independently assessed arterial contrast, venous contamination, overall image quality, and diagnostic evaluability. Statistical analysis included unpaired t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Fisher's exact tests with multiple-comparison correction. RESULTS: 260 patients were included (mean age 56.3 ± 24 years; 90 female). Dedicated CTA demonstrated significantly higher attenuation in all segments except the cervical internal carotid artery (ICA) (p = 0.08). Mean and median attenuation exceeded 250 HU in all segments for both protocols. Measurements <250 HU were more frequent with split-bolus WBCT, reaching significance only in the petrous ICA (p = 0.02). Subjectively, dedicated CTA showed higher arterial contrast and less venous contamination (both p < 0.01), whereas overall image quality varied across readers. Diagnostic evaluability was high in both cohorts, with no significant differences in four of five readers. CONCLUSIONS: Despite lower arterial enhancement, split-bolus WBCT provided adequate cervicocerebral arterial opacification and high diagnostic evaluability, supporting feasibility for initial vascular assessment in polytrauma. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: The findings support the feasibility of split-bolus WBCT for initial cervicocerebral vascular assessment in polytrauma patients.

articles.title: Quantitative Hepatobiliary MRI for Early Prognostic Assessment After Liver Transplantation: Survival Prediction Using the Contrast Enhancement Index.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of the contrast enhancement index (CEI) derived from gadobenate dimeglumine (Gd-BOPTA)-enhanced hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for early assessment of liver graft function after liver transplantation (LT). METHODS: This retrospective study included LT recipients undergoing Gd-BOPTA-enhanced MRI within 6 months after transplantation. CEI was calculated using liver-to-psoas signal intensity ratios on pre-contrast and HBP images acquired 90-120 minutes after contrast administration. ROC, Kaplan-Meier, and age-adjusted Cox regression analyses evaluated associations with mortality. RESULTS: Seventy patients (median age, 62 years; interquartile range [IQR], 48-74) were included. CEI was quantifiable in all cases (median, 1.27; IQR, 1.09-1.37). Non-survivors had significantly lower CEI values than survivors (median, 1.17 vs 1.31; p = 0.03; Cliff's δ = -0.28). ROC analysis showed moderate discrimination for mortality (AUC, 0.667; 95% CI, 0.529-0.793), with an optimal cutoff of 1.301 (sensitivity, 88%; specificity, 51.2%). Patients with CEI <1.301 had significantly lower overall survival (log-rank p = 0.028). After adjustment for recipient age, CEI remained associated with mortality (HR per 0.1-unit increase, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.98; p = 0.035). CONCLUSION: Quantitative CEI measurement on Gd-BOPTA HBP MRI is feasible after LT, and lower CEI values. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This study links quantitative Gd-BOPTA-enhanced HBP MRI with overall survival after LT, supporting CEI as a potential non-invasive imaging biomarker for postoperative risk stratification.

articles.title: Spectral-habitat analysis and perfusion fingerprinting on contrast-enhanced ultrasound for characterizing tumor perfusion in breast lesions.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop a short-time Fourier transform (STFT)-based perfusion fingerprinting method combined with spectral-habitat analysis for characterizing pixel-wise perfusion heterogeneity on contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) and to evaluate its ability to differentiate benign and malignant breast lesions. METHODS: Pixel-wise CEUS time-series data were transformed into the time-frequency domain using STFT. Principal component analysis (PCA) was then applied to reduce the dimensionality of STFT-derived features and generate perfusion fingerprinting maps that preserved spatial and temporal perfusion information. Spectral-habitat maps were generated using K-means clustering to identify perfusion-related tumor subregions. A triple-branch multi-layer fusion model was constructed to integrate full-region and habitat-derived features for lesion classification. To provide an exploratory conventional CEUS quantitative baseline, TIC-derived perfusion features were additionally extracted and evaluated using machine learning classifiers. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, decision curve analysis (DCA), and confusion matrix. RESULTS: The proposed STFT-based perfusion fingerprinting method enabled a more comprehensive characterization of tumor perfusion heterogeneity by preserving pixel-wise spatiotemporal dynamics of CEUS signals. CEUS-derived spectral-habitat maps provided visual representations of intratumoral perfusion heterogeneity and improved the interpretability of the model outputs. In this cohort, the triple-branch multi-layer fusion model achieved an AUC of 0.953, with accuracy of 0.909, precision of 0.907, recall of 0.925, and F1 score of 0.912. Exploratory TIC-based conventional CEUS models achieved AUCs ranging from 0.7677 to 0.8186. DCA suggested potential clinical utility of the proposed model across a range of threshold probabilities, and confusion matrix analysis showed favorable classification performance. CONCLUSION: The STFT-based perfusion fingerprinting method combined with spectral-habitat analysis provides a promising CEUS-based framework for characterizing perfusion heterogeneity in breast lesions. By preserving pixel-wise spatiotemporal information, this approach may provide complementary quantitative information for more interpretable differentiation between benign and malignant lesions.

articles.title: CT-guided biopsy of pulmonary ground-glass nodules: core-needle biopsy versus fine-needle aspiration.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the diagnostic performance and complication profiles of CT-guided core-needle biopsy (CNB) and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for pulmonary ground-glass nodules (GGNs). METHODS: Consecutive patients who underwent CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of pulmonary GGNs between January 2021 and August 2022 were screened. Of 657 patients assessed, 538 were included (CNB, n = 448; FNA, n = 90). Six FNA results classified as atypical cells were considered indeterminate and excluded from binary diagnostic-performance analyses, leaving 532 classifiable cases. Final diagnoses were established by surgical pathology or imaging follow-up of at least 12 months. Diagnostic performance was compared without adjustment, whereas complication outcomes were assessed using multivariable logistic regression and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). RESULTS: Among the 532 classifiable biopsies, the overall accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were 93.2%, 91.4%, and 100.0%, respectively, based on the available composite reference standard. CNB showed higher unadjusted accuracy than FNA (94.6% vs. 85.7%, P = 0.007) and higher sensitivity (93.2% vs. 82.4%, P = 0.008). In the full cohort of 538 procedures, multivariable analysis showed that CNB was associated with higher odds of intrapulmonary hemorrhage (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 2.91; P < 0.001) and hemoptysis (aOR: 3.07; P < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant association was observed for pneumothorax. CONCLUSION: CT-guided percutaneous biopsy yielded determinate diagnostic results for most pulmonary GGNs under the available composite reference standard. In unadjusted comparisons, CNB showed higher diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity than FNA but was associated with greater risks of hemorrhagic complications. Given the lack of adjustment for baseline differences in diagnostic-performance analyses, the apparent diagnostic advantage of CNB should be interpreted cautiously. Biopsy technique should be individualized according to lesion characteristics and patient-specific risks.

articles.title: Clinical-MRI-IVIM combined model for differentiating thymic epithelial tumors from anterior mediastinal lymphoma in large masses.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic value of clinical and intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) parameters for differentiating large anterior mediastinal invasive masses (≥ 3 cm), particularly thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) and lymphomas. METHODS: This prospective study included 92 patients (mean age, 44.8 ± 15.5 years) with pathologically confirmed TETs (n = 52) or lymphomas (n = 40) who underwent routine MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging, and IVIM sequences. Quantitative parameters, including the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), true diffusion coefficient (D), pseudo-diffusion coefficient (D*), and perfusion fraction (f), were measured. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to construct predictive models. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, with area under the curve (AUC) compared by the DeLong test. Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling, and multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors. RESULTS: Compared with TET, lymphoma was associated with younger age, higher female proportion, higher LDH, larger volume, more frequent pleural and/or lung invasion, and higher D * values (all p < 0.05). Age, sex, LDH level, lung and/or pleural infiltration, and f in the IVIM model were risk predictive factors for distinguishing lymphoma from TET. Among all models, the clinical MRI-IVM model achieved the highest diagnostic performance numerically (AUC = 0.946, 95% CI: 0.901-0.991); However, compared with the clinical MRI model (AUC = 0.929, 95% CI: 0.873-0.985), the increment brought by adding IVIM parameters was not significant (DeLong test, P = 0.316). Calibration analysis showed good consistency between predicted probabilities. The apparent AUC of Bootstrap's internal validation was 0.946, the estimation deviation was 0.017, and the standard error was 0.022, indicating limited optimism in the model's performance. CONCLUSIONS: The clinical-MRI-IVIM model had shown relatively good diagnostic performance in preoperative differentiation of large anterior mediastinal TETs and lymphoma. However, there is no statistical difference in the increment benefit generated by IVIM parameters in the composite model. Therefore, in order to elucidate the clinical efficacy of IVIM, further large-scale, prospective, and multi-center studies are necessary.

articles.title: Combined Metasurface and Metamaterial Passive Transmit Lens and Receive Array for 3 T.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Metasurfaces (MSs) and metamaterials (MMs) can reduce transmit field nulls caused by wavelength effects at higher MR field strengths. We present a layered MM and MS resonant structure that improves transmit field performance when used as a combined slab (i.e., the metaslab), while also operating as a receive array. METHODS: The MS structure consists of cross-shaped traces joined by capacitors on a PCB. It is embedded between two layers of a MM consisting of inductively coupled longitudinal strips acting as a 2D transmission line. The two structures are intrinsically decoupled and support connection ports to create an 8-element receive array. Simulations were performed with a realistic body phantom, and imaging experiments were performed at 3 T on a large water phantom and in vivo on an adult male's abdomen. RESULTS: Transmit efficiency is improved by a factor of 1.45 in simulation over body coil alone using a realistic body model and by a factor of 1.55 from in vivo measurement.
